#| label: setup
#| include: false
set.seed(2026)
# non-ASCII characters in output and plots under a "C" locale
invisible(Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "C.UTF-8"))
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")

A box holds 25 light bulbs, 3 of which are defective. We take two without replacement. What is the probability that both are defective? We could count with [combinations](../combinations/index.qmd), but there is a more natural route: think **step by step**, the way the experiment happens.

## The rule for two events

From the definition of [conditional probability](../conditional-probability/index.qmd), $P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B)/P(A)$, multiplying by $P(A)$ gives the **multiplication rule**:

$$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A).$$

For both to happen, $A$ must happen first, and **then**, given $A$, $B$ must happen.

For the bulbs, let $A$ = {the 1st is defective} and $B$ = {the 2nd is defective}. Then $P(A) = 3/25$. If the 1st was defective, 24 bulbs remain with 2 defective, so $P(B \mid A) = 2/24$. Hence

$$P(A \cap B) = \frac{3}{25} \cdot \frac{2}{24} = \frac{1}{100}.$$

Combinations give the same: $\binom{3}{2} / \binom{25}{2} = 3/300 = 1/100$.

## Many steps

Applying the rule again and again, for any events $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$:

$$\begin{aligned}
P(A_1 \cap A_2 \cap \cdots \cap A_n) = {} & P(A_1) \cdot P(A_2 \mid A_1) \cdot P(A_3 \mid A_1 \cap A_2) \\
& \cdots P(A_n \mid A_1 \cap \cdots \cap A_{n-1}).
\end{aligned}$$

Each factor is the probability of the next step, **given all the earlier ones**. The same rule holds when everything is conditioned on an event $\Gamma$ with $P(\Gamma) > 0$::

$$P(A \cap B \mid \Gamma) = P(A \mid \Gamma) \cdot P(B \mid A \cap \Gamma).$$

The birthday problem, which we solved with [arrangements](../permutations-arrangements/index.qmd), is an example: the 2nd person's birthday differs from the 1st with probability $364/365$, the 3rd's from the first two with $363/365$, and so on.

## The probability tree

The rule becomes a picture in a **probability tree**: each branch carries the conditional probability of its step, and the probability of a path is the **product** of its branches. For an event made of several paths, we **add** their probabilities, since the paths are disjoint.

In the tree below we draw balls from an urn with red (R) and green (G) balls. Change the contents, the number of draws and replacement, and pick an event.

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Probability tree: draws from an urn
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof r22 = Inputs.range([1, 8], {label: "Red", step: 1, value: 3})
viewof g22 = Inputs.range([1, 8], {label: "Green", step: 1, value: 5})
viewof k22 = Inputs.radio([2, 3], {label: "Draws", value: 3})
viewof rep22 = Inputs.toggle({label: "With replacement", value: false})
viewof ev22 = Inputs.select(new Map([
  ["All red", s => !s.includes("G")],
  ["Exactly one red", s => [...s].filter(c => c === "R").length === 1],
  ["At least one red", s => s.includes("R")],
  ["The 2nd is red", s => s[1] === "R"]
]), {label: "Event"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const gcd = (a, b) => b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a;
  const fr = (n, d) => { if (n === 0) return "0"; const g = gcd(n, d); return d / g === 1 ? `${n / g}` : `${n / g}/${d / g}`; };
  const k = (rep22 || r22 + g22 >= 3) ? k22 : 2, leaves = [], edges = [];
  // recursively: every node has an R branch and a G branch
  const rec = (seq, r, g, num, den) => {
    if (seq.length === k) { leaves.push({seq, num, den}); return; }
    [["R", r], ["G", g]].forEach(([c, cnt]) => {
      const tot = r + g;
      const n2 = num * cnt, d2 = den * tot;
      edges.push({from: seq, to: seq + c, label: fr(cnt, tot), zero: cnt === 0});
      const nr = rep22 ? r : r - (c === "R" ? 1 : 0), ng = rep22 ? g : g - (c === "G" ? 1 : 0);
      rec(seq + c, nr, ng, n2, d2);
    });
  };
  rec("", r22, g22, 1, 1);
  const nL = leaves.length, row = 44, W = 560, H = nL * row + 20;
  const colX = d => 20 + d * (380 / k);
  const yOf = new Map();
  leaves.forEach((l, i) => yOf.set(l.seq, 15 + i * row + row / 2));
  const nodeY = s => d3.mean(leaves.filter(l => l.seq.startsWith(s)), l => yOf.get(l.seq));
  const inEv = l => ev22(l.seq);
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", `0 0 ${W} ${H}`).style("width", "100%").style("max-width", W + "px").style("font", "18px sans-serif");
  edges.forEach(e => {
    const x1 = colX(e.from.length), y1 = nodeY(e.from), x2 = colX(e.to.length), y2 = nodeY(e.to);
    const hot = leaves.some(l => l.seq.startsWith(e.to) && inEv(l) && l.num > 0);
    svg.append("line").attr("x1", x1).attr("y1", y1).attr("x2", x2).attr("y2", y2)
      .attr("stroke", e.zero ? "#ddd" : hot ? "#f28e2b" : "#9ecae1").attr("stroke-width", hot ? 2.5 : 1.3);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", (x1 + x2) / 2).attr("y", (y1 + y2) / 2 - 4).attr("text-anchor", "middle")
      .attr("fill", e.zero ? "#bbb" : "#2c5a8a").style("font-size", "16px").text(e.label);
    svg.append("text").attr("x", x2 + 4).attr("y", y2).attr("dy", "0.35em").attr("fill", e.to.endsWith("R") ? "#c62828" : "#2e7d32").attr("font-weight", "bold").text(e.to.slice(-1));
  });
  svg.append("circle").attr("cx", colX(0)).attr("cy", nodeY("")).attr("r", 6).attr("fill", "#4e79a7");
  leaves.forEach(l => {
    const y = yOf.get(l.seq), on = inEv(l) && l.num > 0;
    svg.append("text").attr("x", 430).attr("y", y).attr("dy", "0.35em").attr("fill", on ? "#c25e00" : (l.num ? "#333" : "#bbb")).attr("font-weight", on ? "bold" : null)
      .text(`${l.seq}: ${fr(l.num, l.den)}`);
  });
  const evL = leaves.filter(l => inEv(l) && l.num > 0);
  const D = leaves[0].den;
  const tot = evL.reduce((s, l) => s + l.num * (D / l.den), 0);
  const val = tot / D;
  return html`${svg.node()}<div class="ix-note">Orange: the paths of the event. Each path is a product of branches, and the event is the sum of its paths:<br>
    <b>P = ${evL.length > 1 ? evL.map(l => fr(l.num, l.den)).join(" + ") + " = " : ""}${fr(tot, D)} ≈ ${val.toLocaleString("en-GB", {maximumFractionDigits: 4})}</b></div>`;
}
```
:::

Compare "The 2nd is red" with and without replacement. Without replacement the branches of the 2nd step change, yet the result is again $r/(r+g)$, the same as for the 1st ball. This is no coincidence, and we will explain it with total probability two posts from now.

## The LOTTO cards

Seven cards carry the letters L, L, O, O, O, T, T. We shuffle them, draw five and lay them in a row. What is the probability that they spell LOTTO?

We follow the word letter by letter. The 1st card must be an L: 2 out of 7. Given that, the 2nd must be an O: 3 of the remaining 6. Continuing:

$$P(\text{LOTTO}) = \frac{2}{7} \cdot \frac{3}{6} \cdot \frac{2}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{2}{3} = \frac{24}{2{,}520} = \frac{1}{105} \approx 0.0095.$$

```{r}
#| label: lotto-cards
cards <- c("L", "L", "O", "O", "O", "T", "T")
target <- c("L", "O", "T", "T", "O")
hits <- replicate(100000, all(sample(cards, 5) == target))
c(simulation = mean(hits), exact = 1 / 105)
```

Draw some cards yourself. The table shows, step by step, the probability of the right letter given the earlier ones:

::: {.ix-panel}
::: {.ix-title}
Will the cards spell LOTTO?
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof one22 = Inputs.button("Draw 5 cards")
viewof many22 = Inputs.button("1,000 attempts")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
lotto22 = {
  const deck = [..."LLOOOTT"], target = [..."LOTTO"];
  const draw = () => d3.shuffle(deck.slice()).slice(0, 5);
  return {deck, target, draw};
}
manyRes22 = { many22; if (many22 === 0) return null; let k = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) if (lotto22.draw().join("") === "LOTTO") k++; return k; }
{
  one22;
  const {deck, target} = lotto22, hand = lotto22.draw();
  const rows = [];
  let left = deck.slice(), prod = 1, alive = true;
  target.forEach((t, i) => {
    const need = left.filter(c => c === t).length, n = left.length, p = need / n;
    if (alive) prod *= p;
    const ok = hand[i] === t;
    rows.push(html`<tr><td>${i + 1}</td><td><b>${t}</b></td><td>${need}/${n}</td>
      <td><span style="display:inline-block;width:1.8em;text-align:center;border:1px solid ${ok && alive ? "#2e7d32" : "#c62828"};border-radius:4px;background:${ok && alive ? "#e8f5e9" : "#fdecea"}">${hand[i]}</span></td></tr>`);
    if (alive && !ok) alive = false;
    left.splice(left.indexOf(t), 1);
  });
  const win = hand.join("") === "LOTTO";
  return html`<table class="ix-tbl"><tr><th>Step</th><th>Need</th><th>P(right)</th><th>Card</th></tr>${rows}</table>
    <div class="ix-note">Product: 2/7 · 3/6 · 2/5 · 1/4 · 2/3 = <b>1/105</b>. This time: <b>${hand.join("")}</b> ${win ? html`<span class="ix-ok">✓ LOTTO!</span>` : html`<span class="ix-no">✗</span>`}
    ${manyRes22 !== null ? html`<br>In 1,000 attempts: <b>${manyRes22}</b> successes (about 9.5 expected).` : ""}</div>`;
}
```
:::

In the table the "Need" column always shows the right letter, and the probabilities are computed **as if all earlier letters had come out right**. That is exactly what the rule says: each factor is conditioned on the earlier steps.

If we ask not whether the cards spell the word but whether they **can** spell it (in any order), order does not matter and we use combinations: we need 1 of the 2 Ls, 2 of the 3 Os and both Ts, so

$$\frac{\binom{2}{1}\binom{3}{2}\binom{2}{2}}{\binom{7}{5}} = \frac{6}{21} = \frac{2}{7}.$$

## Key takeaways

- **Multiplication rule:** $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A)$.
- For many steps, multiply the probability of each step, conditioned on all the earlier ones.
- In a **probability tree**, multiply along a path and add the paths of an event.
- Without replacement the probabilities change from step to step. With replacement they stay the same.

## Review questions

**1. Quick quiz.**

::: {.ix-panel}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz22 = [
  {q: "We draw two cards from a 52-card deck without replacement. What is the probability that both are aces?",
   opts: ["(4/52)²", "4/52 · 3/51", "2/52", "4/52 + 3/51"], ans: 1,
   why: "P(1st ace) = 4/52 and, given that, P(2nd ace) = 3/51. The product is 1/221."},
  {q: "In a probability tree, how do we get the probability of an event made of two paths?",
   opts: ["Multiply the two paths", "Add the two paths", "Take the larger one"], ans: 1,
   why: "Each path is a product of branches. The paths are disjoint, so their probabilities add."},
  {q: "Three people. What is the probability that all their birthdays differ (365 equally likely days)?",
   opts: ["364/365 · 363/365", "(364/365)²", "3/365", "1 − 3/365"], ans: 0,
   why: "The 1st can have any day. The 2nd differs from the 1st with probability 364/365, and the 3rd from the first two with 363/365."},
  {q: "Which is the correct multiplication rule?",
   opts: ["P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B)", "P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B | A)", "P(A ∩ B) = P(A | B) · P(A)", "P(A ∩ B) = P(B | A) / P(A)"], ans: 1,
   why: "P(A) · P(B) holds only for independent events, the subject of the next post. It is also true that P(A ∩ B) = P(B) · P(A | B)."}
]
{
  const root = html`<div></div>`, score = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`, done = new Map();
  quiz22.forEach((item, k) => {
    const fb = html`<div class="ix-note"></div>`;
    const btns = item.opts.map(o => html`<button>${o}</button>`);
    const opts = html`<div style="margin:4px 0 0 6px">${btns.map((b, j) => {
      b.onclick = () => {
        const ok = j === item.ans; done.set(k, ok);
        btns.forEach(x => x.className = "");
        b.className = ok ? "ix-picked-ok" : "ix-picked-no";
        fb.innerHTML = (ok ? `<span class="ix-ok">✓ Correct.</span> ` : `<span class="ix-no">✗ Not quite.</span> `) + item.why;
        score.innerHTML = `<b>Correct: ${[...done.values()].filter(x => x).length} of ${quiz22.length}</b>`;
      };
      return b;
    })}</div>`;
    root.append(html`<div style="margin:12px 0"><div>${k + 1}. ${item.q}</div>${opts}${fb}</div>`);
  });
  root.append(score);
  return root;
}
```
:::

**2.** From the box of 25 bulbs (3 defective) we take three without replacement. What is the probability that none is defective? Solve with the multiplication rule and check with combinations.

**3.** We roll a die until a 6 appears. What is the probability that exactly three rolls are needed?

**4.** Modify the R code to estimate the probability that the five cards **can** spell LOTTO.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

2. $\dfrac{22}{25} \cdot \dfrac{21}{24} \cdot \dfrac{20}{23} = \dfrac{9{,}240}{13{,}800} \approx$ `r fmt(22/25 * 21/24 * 20/23, 3)`. With combinations: $\binom{22}{3} / \binom{25}{3} = 1{,}540 / 2{,}300$, the same.
3. The first two rolls are not 6 and the third is: $\dfrac{5}{6} \cdot \dfrac{5}{6} \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{25}{216} \approx 0.116$.
4. `mean(replicate(100000, all(sort(sample(cards, 5)) == sort(target))))` gives about 0.286, that is $2/7$.
:::
